q: [70th BPSC] A proclamation of National Emergency under Article 352 can be made only on the written recommendation of:
explanation: 44th Amdt: the Union Cabinet's written recommendation is mandatory (1975's oral-advice lesson). The PM alone cannot trigger it — the whole Cabinet must be on record.

q: The grounds for National Emergency after the 44th Amendment include:
options: War, external aggression and internal disturbance
Breakdown of law and order only
War, external aggression and armed rebellion
explanation: 44th (1978): 'armed rebellion' replaced 'internal disturbance' (too vague, abused in 1975). War/external aggression/armed rebellion — and the President may act even on imminent danger.

q: A proclamation of National Emergency must be approved by Parliament within:
explanation: 44th: 1 month (was 2 months), special majority, both Houses; otherwise it lapses. Extensions: every 6 months indefinitely — each needs fresh approval.

q: National Emergency has been proclaimed in India:
explanation: 3 times: 1962 (China war), 1971 (Pak war), 1975 (internal disturbance — the only non-war one; revoked 1977).

q: Financial Emergency under Article 360:
options: Has never been imposed; once approved, it continues indefinitely without periodic re-approval
Lasts a maximum of six months
explanation: Art 360: never imposed; approval within 2 months by simple majority; no maximum duration — continues till revoked. 69th BPSC (Q118-119) tested exactly this never-used status.

q: Under Art 358, Article 19 is automatically suspended:
options: Only when the emergency is on the ground of war or external aggression — not armed rebellion
explanation: Art 358: Art 19 stands suspended only for war/external aggression emergencies — the 44th's refinement (1975-type internal emergencies no longer touch Art 19). Art 359 is the separate order-based route.

q: Which Fundamental Rights can NEVER be suspended even during an Emergency?
explanation: 44th Amdt: Arts 20-21 non-suspendable under any presidential order (Art 359's bar) — the anti-ADM-Jabalpur codification (that 1976 case was formally overruled in Puttaswamy, 2017).

q: President's Rule under Art 356 can last a maximum of:
explanation: 6 months at a time, extendable to 3 years max; beyond 1 year only if a National Emergency is in force or the EC certifies elections can't be held (44th's brakes).

q: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) established:
options: Art 356 is judicially reviewable; majority must be tested on the floor; no dissolution before parliamentary approval
explanation: Bommai (1994): floor test; judicial review; assembly dissolution only after Parliament approves; secularism = basic structure. Bihar's Rameshwar Prasad (2006) applied it to strike the dissolution.

q: The 1975 National Emergency was proclaimed on the ground of:
explanation: June 1975: 'internal disturbance' (the pre-44th term) — triggered amid JP's Bihar-rooted movement; the 44th later renamed the ground 'armed rebellion' precisely to prevent such use.

q: The Lok Sabha may require reconsideration of a National Emergency by a special sitting if:
options: One-tenth of LS members demand it in writing — the House must sit within 14 days
explanation: Art 352(8)-(9) (44th): 1/10 of LS members may demand a special sitting to consider revocation; if passed by simple majority, the Emergency stands revoked — LS's anti-emergency check.

q: During a National Emergency, the Lok Sabha's term can be extended:
options: By 1 year at a time (any number of times while the Emergency lasts)
explanation: LS term: extendable 1 year at a time under a National Emergency (not beyond 6 months after it ends). State assemblies: 6 months at a time (Art 172).

q: Under Art 360, during a Financial Emergency, the President may direct:
options: Reduction of salaries of all state and Union employees, including Supreme Court and High Court judges
explanation: Art 360: salary-reduction directions (including judges' salaries per 360(4)(b)); money-bills reservation for the President; financial propriety observance. The judge-salary clause is the classic MCQ point.

q: Bihar's Assembly dissolution (2005) was struck down because:
options: The Governor's report was mala fide; the floor test was bypassed
explanation: Rameshwar Prasad (2006): Governor Buta Singh's recommendation was mala fide (no floor test, no chance to form a government) — Bommai principles applied to Bihar's 2005 dissolution.

q: Under Art 359, the President may suspend the enforcement of:
options: Named fundamental rights — except Arts 20 and 21
explanation: Art 359: presidential order suspends enforcement of specified FRs (not the rights themselves); Arts 20-21 exempt (44th). Art 358 is automatic; 359 needs an order naming rights.

q: Art 365 deals with:
options: Failure to comply with Union directions — deemed failure of constitutional machinery
explanation: Art 365: a state's failure to comply with the Union's executive directions = deemed 'failure of constitutional machinery' → Art 356 available — the backdoor trigger.

q: The proclamation of President's Rule must be approved by Parliament within:
explanation: Art 356: approval within 2 months by simple majority (both Houses); continues 6 months per approval, max 3 years. Contrast 352's 1-month/special-majority rule.

q: During a National Emergency, the Centre's executive power extends to:
options: Any matter on which the Union has power to legislate — including State List directions to states
explanation: Art 353: the Union may direct states on any matter; Parliament may legislate on State List subjects (Art 250) — the 'unitary conversion' of the federation (Art 353/250/354 combo).

q: Which state experienced President's Rule when Jharkhand was carved out of it (2000)?
explanation: Bihar was under President's Rule (1999-2000, the Rabri Devi dismissal's aftermath) when the Bihar Reorganisation Act 2000 created Jharkhand (Nov 15, 2000) — a rare reorganisation-during-356 episode.

q: The 44th Amendment's emergency-package changes include all EXCEPT:
options: One-month approval window with special majority
Removal of the LS's power to revoke the Emergency by resolution
explanation: The 44th ADDED the LS's 1/10-members special-sitting + simple-majority revocation (Art 352(7)-(8)) — it did not remove it. A/B/C are the 44th's actual signature changes.

q: 'Samvidhan Hatya Diwas' commemorates:
options: The proclamation of the 1975 Emergency (25 June)
explanation: June 25 declared Samvidhan Hatya Diwas (2024) marking the 1975 Emergency's proclamation — the 50th anniversary fell in June 2025, keeping the topic exam-fresh.

q: During President's Rule in a state, the dissolved/suspended assembly's fate and Parliament's role:
options: The Union Parliament exercises the state legislature's powers; the assembly may be dissolved only after parliamentary approval of the proclamation
The President legislates directly without Parliament
explanation: During 356: Parliament (or the President, when Parliament not in session, subject to approval) exercises the state's legislative powers; Bommai: no dissolution before Parliament approves the proclamation.

q: Who decides whether a National Emergency proclamation deserves revocation?
options: The President anytime; AND the Lok Sabha by simple majority (if 1/10 members demand a sitting)
explanation: Dual revocation: the President's revocation anytime (no approval needed) + LS's resolution route (1/10 demand → special sitting within 14 days → simple majority = revoked).

q: The JP Movement (1974) and the 1975 Emergency are linked because:
options: JP's Total Revolution — launched from Bihar — challenged the Indira government; the Emergency was proclaimed citing internal disturbance amid JP's 'army' call and the Allahabad verdict
Bihar was exempted from the Emergency
The Emergency helped JP win elections
explanation: JP's Bihar-born movement (1974 Gujarat + Bihar agitations → Total Revolution) + the June 1975 Allahabad HC verdict = the Emergency's immediate triggers; JP was arrested — the Bihar-history/polity crossover BPSC loves.

q: Financial Emergency directions under Art 360(4) include all EXCEPT:
options: Reservation of state money bills for the President
Salary cuts for state employees, including SC/HC judges
explanation: Art 360(4): salary-reduction directions + money-bill reservation — NOT the FC's dissolution (the FC is a constitutional body under Art 280; no emergency power touches it).
